title: The Languages of the Holy Bible
subtitle: Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek in the Scriptures
author: Juan María Tellería Larrañaga
description: A pedagogical introduction to the languages in which the Bible was written, to enrich the reading and study of the Holy Scriptures.

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.subtitle: Why the original languages matter
lessons.summary: The Bible came to light through a long process of gathering traditions, composing the earliest documents, and producing a definitive text, sometimes with later corrections and/or additions that took place either in very ancient times or throughout the centuries of the Middle Ages, when monks copied and recopied the Sacred Texts in order to preserve them. content:
The Bible came to light through a long process of gathering 
traditions, composing the earliest documents, and 
producing a definitive text, sometimes with later corrections and/or additions 
that took place either in very ancient times, or 
throughout the centuries of the Middle Ages, when monks 
copied and recopied the Sacred Texts in order to preserve them. That 
meant it was not always written in the same language.  
 It is a well-known fact that the thirty-nine 
canonical writings of the Old Testament were composed in Hebrew, the 
language of ancient Israel, although in certain later books, from the time 
of the Babylonian captivity or afterward, some chapters 
or isolated words are found in Aramaic, the vehicle of expression 
adopted by the Jews from that time onward. On the other hand, the 
New Testament was written entirely in Greek. Also surviving 
in Greek are the so-called deuterocanonical books (or 
“apocrypha”) of the Old Testament that are found today in 
Catholic and interconfessional versions of the Holy Bible. 
 This means that knowledge of these ancient languages is 
highly necessary for anyone undertaking specialized studies of 
the Holy Scriptures. That is why in seminaries, biblical institutes, 
and faculties of theology courses are generally offered 
in biblical languages, especially Hebrew and Greek, so that 
future ministers of the gospel may acquire certain skills that will 
be useful in their work of exposition and explanation of the 
word of God. That is also why our lay readers should 
have in their academic background some very general notions 
of how these languages worked, what their history and 
development were, or how they were written. This knowledge will complement their 
L 
2

formation and will benefit them and those whom they 
serve in their respective parishes. 
 We add below the basic information needed on 
the biblical languages in this order:

lessons.title: The Hebrew Language
lessons.subtitle: Origin, classification, and writing

content:
This designation traditionally refers to the language in which 
most of the Old Testament was written, 
understood as the mother tongue of the ancient Hebrews 
descended from Jacob, the twelve tribes of Israel, especially 
from the time of the conquest of Canaan. Curiously, the 
Old Testament never refers to this language by this name, 
but rather mentions it as the «language of Canaan» or 
«Canaanite» (sephath Kenaán, in Isa. 19:18), or simply «Jewish» 
(yehudith. cf. 2 Kgs. 18:26,28; Isa. 36:11,13; 2 Chr. 32:18; Neh. 13:24, though 
in this last text it probably refers to Aramaic). Strictly speaking, 
«Jewish» or «the Jewish language» indicates the language of the kingdom of 
Judah, which became prominent after the deportation of the ten 
northern tribes to Assyria. It is in the later Greek literature of the Jews 
that the name «Hebrew» is first applied to the 
language of the Jews, as in the prologue of the deuterocanonical book 
of Ecclesiasticus, where we read the adverb hebraistí, that is, «in 
Hebrew», and in the work of the first-century Jewish writer Flavius 
Josephus, who expressly mentions the glossa ton Hebraîon or «language 
of the Hebrews». The New Testament refers to the «language of the 
Hebrews», in Greek hebraíon dialektós, in contrast with the language of the 
Hellenistic Jews, although it does not refer exactly to the ancient 
Hebrew language, but to the vernacular Aramaic dialect of Palestine at that 
time. Today, with the term ibrit, that is, «Hebrew», one 
designates the official language of the present state of Israel.

The Hebrew language belongs to the great family of 
Semitic languages, classified by linguists into three large groups:

1. Northeastern Semitic, in which one language stands out that attained 
great importance in the ancient world, Akkadian or Accadian, the language 
of the great empire of King Sargon (3rd millennium B.C.), which we find 
extensively documented in cuneiform writing. Within it are 
distinguished two important dialects, Babylonian and Assyrian. 
S 
4

2. Northwestern Semitic, in which we highlight two large 
linguistic branches: the first is Aramaic, one of whose most 
important variants would later be known as Syriac. Aramaic came 
to be the great international language of the Fertile Crescent from the 
8th–7th centuries B.C. until approximately the 3rd century B.C., when it was 
replaced by Greek; the second branch is Canaanite, 
within which we include dialects closely related to one another, 
such as «Hebrew» proper, Phoenician, Moabite, Ammonite, 
and Edomite.

3. Southern Semitic, in which we highlight Arabic and Ethiopic, 
with their immense dialectal varieties. Arabic is, without doubt, the 
most important and most outstanding language of the entire Semitic stock, 
because of its internal structure, which keeps it very close to ancient 
Semitic, and because of its spread throughout the world from the expansion of 
Islam in the 7th century of our era.

Of this whole broad linguistic family there survive today as 
living languages Arabic, Ethiopic, Syriac (the language of the Christians of 
Syria, most of whom currently reside in the U.S.), 
modern «Hebrew», and remnants of ancient Phoenician (which survive in 
Maltese, the official language of the Republic of Malta).

The history of the Hebrew language is divided into three stages, which 
traditionally receive the following names:

1. Ancient or Biblical Hebrew. It covers an approximate period of 
about a thousand years, subdivided in turn into an earlier period, 
up to 500 B.C., and a more recent one that reaches the 1st century B.C. The 
sources available to us for knowing it are, besides the 
Old Testament, the Gezer agricultural calendar (10th century B.C.), the 
Samaria ostraca (8th century B.C.), the Jerusalem inscriptions 
of Siloam and of Shebna (around 700 B.C.), the Wadi 
Murabba’at 17 palimpsest (8th/7th centuries B.C.), the Lachish ostraca (around 600 
B.C.), and a whole series of coins, seals, or weights that contain some 
written word or other. The archaeologists’ pickaxe continues 
untiringly to bring to light objects that contain inscriptions or 
words in ancient Hebrew from these past centuries. Interesting also for 
5

the study of this period of the language’s history is 
all the rich and extensive literature from Qumran, which shows us 
interesting stages in the evolution of the language.  
In the earlier period, Hebrew is the proper language of the 
Israelites, assimilated by them from the conquest of Canaan. The 
ancestors of Israel, according to Deut. 26:5, must have been Aramaic-speaking. 
Biblical Hebrew, like any living language, must have been 
fragmented into dialects, something of which the Scriptures give us a 
brief glimpse in Judges 12:6 and in Hos. 14:9. In the more recent period, 
on the other hand, after the Babylonian captivity, it is gradually replaced 
by Aramaic as the popular language and its use is relegated to the priestly 
caste, certain aristocratic Jerusalem families, perhaps 
some religious groups with integrist tendencies, and above all, the 
rabbinic schools. Thus the language enters its second historical stage, 
the so-called

2. Middle or Mishnaic Hebrew. It covers the period from the 
1st century B.C. to the 13th century A.D. It takes refuge in the rabbinic schools 
and is enormously simplified because of its restricted use and the 
quantity of Aramaisms and Hellenisms it assimilates. It is in 
reality a lingua scholastica without popular support, whose sources 
for us are the Mishnah, the Tosefta, and the midrashim on the 
sacred texts. In this stage, more specifically in the 7th century 
A.D., the Masoretic vowel system of our current printed Hebrew Bibles 
comes to light. In the 13th century, with the decline of 
Judaism and its schools, Hebrew ceases to be used in 
rabbinic discussions and is replaced by the different languages 
used by the Jews, according to the places where they were 
settled.

3. Neo-Hebrew or ibrit. This name is given to the official language of 
the present State of Israel, which is a Hebrew reconstructed from 
Mishnaic Hebrew in an artificial way by the Zionists of the late 
19th century. At present it has about ten million 
speakers, 95% of whom reside in Israel and the rest are 
scattered among the different Jewish communities of the world. The 
Zionist programs have sought from their beginnings to make 
Hebrew once again a living and flourishing language, the proper language 
of the Jewish people. It would seem that, at least in Israel, this has been achieved. 
6

Needless to say, this Neo-Hebrew is not the Hebrew of the Old 
Testament: its grammar is completely simplified and 
adapted to the structure of Western languages—something that is 
especially evident in the verbal conjugation system—and its 
vocabulary registers a whole series of technical terms and concepts 
proper to our modern world. One must not forget that, 
for centuries, Jews have lived (and a good majority still live) 
in Western countries, so that their mother tongues are 
no longer any Semitic language, but those of the West.

The writing of the Hebrew language is, as everyone knows, 
alphabetic and proceeds from right to left, in the opposite direction from 
ours. The Hebrew alephbet currently in use, so designated by the 
name of its first letter, áleph, is the one commonly known 
as the square alephbet or Aramaic alephbet. It has been used since at least 
the 1st century B.C. and is the one that appears in the biblical texts in use and in 
current ibrit in printed texts. It contains 22 exclusively 
consonantal signs, without distinctions of uppercase and lowercase, and which 
may also be used as numerical signs:

áleph (light glottal aspiration, silent in ibrit) 
 beth (b). In ibrit b, v 
 gimel (voiced g) 
 daleth (d) 
 he (silent h at the end of a word, unless it has an interior point;  
aspirated in other cases) 
 waw (w). In ibrit vav (fricative v) 
 zayin (voiced s) 
 cheth (Spanish j) 
 teth (t) 
 yodh (y) 
7

khaph, with a final form 
  (k, kh) 
 lamed (l) 
 mem, with a final form 
  (m) 
 nun, with a final form 
  (n) 
 samekh (voiceless s) 
 ayin (uvular stroke similar to Arabic ghayin, silent in ibrit) 
 pe, with a final form 
  (p, ph)  
 tsade, with a final form 
  (emphatic s, ts in ibrit) 
 qoph (q) 
 resh (single-tap r) 
 shin (sh), with the graphic variant sin 
  (voiceless s) 
 tau (t, th). In ibrit tav (t)

The final forms 
 , to which Jewish teachers give the 
mnemonic name khamnaphets, can only appear at the end 
of a word. 
Occasionally, some letters of the alephbet appear in the printed text of the Bible 
with an interior point: when they are the stop consonants 
 , those corresponding to the Jewish mnemonic word 
begadkhephath, that is, B G D K P T, that point 
is called dagesh lene and indicates the original stop pronunciation b g d k 
p t, without which the pronunciation would be fricative bh gh dh kh ph th. When 
that point appears in other letters, it receives the name dagesh forte and 
indicates a reduplication of sound. E.g., 
  would be pronounced 
mm, qq, tt, tsts respectively. The consonant 
  only has an interior point, 
called mappiq, 
 , at the end of a word to indicate that it must 
be pronounced. Otherwise, in final position in a word 
  is a 
silent letter.  
Until the end of the 2nd century B.C. the Jews used the alephbet 
traditionally called Phoenician, attested in Palestine from the 
8

9th century B.C. The biblical autographs must therefore have been written 
in this archaic alephbet. At present, ibrit also uses 
a cursive alephbet for handwriting that differs somewhat from the 
square one, and which is generally used in Jewish schools 
throughout the world. 
And what about the vowel letters?, one might ask. Semitic languages do not allow, as Indo-European ones do, the 
accumulation or clustering of consonants on a single vowel 
sound. To each consonantal phoneme there corresponds one vowel 
exclusively, or at most a semivowel. Only at the end of a word 
is a consonant without a vowel conceivable. 
The problem lies, as we have seen, in the fact 
that the Hebrew alephbet does not record vowel letters; it is exclusively 
consonantal, as is also the case in Arabic. The speaker must supply 
the vowels when seeing the written words. We can imagine the 
complication this caused when Hebrew ceased to be the spoken 
language of the Jewish people, replaced by Aramaic, and took refuge in the 
rabbinic schools. Hence the need for a written vowel system 
to aid in the correct reading of the Sacred Texts. The 
Masoretes of the early Middle Ages (7th–9th centuries A.D.) were 
charged with developing it, attempting to reproduce as 
exactly as possible the different vowels of ancient Hebrew that 
oral tradition, it was supposed, had preserved. Since the consonantal 
alephbet was considered sacred and unalterable, it was necessary that 
the vowels be reduced to dots and dashes placed above, below, or 
inside the consonants. It is the system we find in our 
current printed Hebrew Bibles. Some of those Masoretic points 
are not vowels, but equivalents of our punctuation marks, and others are musical notes for liturgical chant in the 
synagogues. The truth is that such a system does not in reality present the 
Hebrew of biblical times, but the liturgical Hebrew of the 
Jewish communities in the midst of which it came to light. It is, therefore, 
subject to objections, for the readings it makes of the 
Old Testament text are not always the best possible. That is why 
specialists point out in very specific cases other more 
accurate variants. In any case, the best current translations of the 
Bible always take into account the Masoretes’ readings, though 
9

they do not disregard other possible ones, such as those of the Greek Septuagint or even 
those of Qumran.

We offer below a summarized outline of the 
grammatical characteristics of Hebrew. 
1. Verb. It is the fundamental part of Hebrew grammar. Hebrew verbal roots 
are for the most part triliteral, that is, 
they contain three basic consonants that must be maintained at all 
times to indicate always the fundamental meaning one 
wishes to convey. If through phonetic changes any of 
those three consonants disappears, this fact has a special value in the 
conjugation. By means of prefixes and suffixes the different 
persons and even the different voices of the verb are formed:  
qal (simple active action)  
niphal (simple passive or reflexive) 
piel (intensive active) 
pual (intensive passive)  
hithpael (intensive reflexive)  
hiphil (causative active)  
hophal (causative passive)  
Thus, e.g., the verbal root qatal, 
 , which means “to kill”, presents the 
following voices: 
qal qatal 
 , that is, “to kill”  
niphal niqtal 
 , that is, “to kill oneself” or “to be killed” 
piel qit·tel 
 , that is, “to murder brutally” 
pual qut·tal 
 , that is, “to be brutally murdered” 
hithpael hithqat·tel 
 , that is, “to commit suicide”  
10

hiphil hiqtil 
 , that is, “to compel to kill”  
hophal hoqtal 
 , “to be compelled to kill”  
(We write only the consonants for greater ease. We do not put 
the Masoretic points. This means that in exclusively consonantal 
writing some forms could be confused.)  
As for verbal tenses, Biblical Hebrew presents a 
system different from that of our Western languages or of modern 
ibrit: it does not have tenses properly speaking, but states; that is, it does not 
emphasize the chronological element, but the kind of action. It presents two 
states, the perfect and the imperfect. The first indicates completed and finished 
action, while the second indicates permanent or unfinished action. Let us see some examples: when in Genesis 
1:1 we read that «in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth», the verbal 
form bará, which is a qal perfect 3rd singular, indicates a 
simple finished action; God created once and for all, He is not 
always creating our world. Likewise, when God says to 
Moses: «I am who I am» (Ex. 3:14), the verbal form ehyeh, which is 
a qal imperfect 1st singular, indicates a permanent action: 
God always is; He has not been once and ceased to be today. That is why 
some have proposed other possible translations of these 
words such as I am who was, I am who will be, I will be who I will be, I 
am who causes to be (understanding that in this verb, because of its 
peculiarities, this form can be either qal or hiphil), etc., 
all of them possible from the standpoint of the language and 
grammar. At times, the biblical authors present several imperfect 
states chained by the copulative conjunction to indicate 
a series of successive actions dependent on a perfect state 
that sets the pattern for the whole (chained perfect states 
dependent on an imperfect are also possible, though less 
frequent). It is the stylistic feature that grammarians call consecutive 
waw (some prefer the name conversive waw), very 
characteristic of Biblical Hebrew, nonexistent in later stages of the 
language. 
Within the field of the imperfect state is what grammarians designate as the voluntative mood, that is, forms that 
express wish, command, or intention: in relation to the first 
persons we find the cohortative, which consists of an imperfect 
11

“lengthened” by the addition of the final syllable –ah, , as when Israel 
asks permission of Edom to cross its land in Num. 21:22, and says 
«let me pass», ebberah; in relation to the second and 
third persons we find the jussive, consisting of an imperfect 
“shortened” by the loss of its last syllable, as when God 
commands in the first Creation account that the light «be», yehí. It is 
important also to note that the jussive, with the negative particle 
al, serves for third-person prohibitions. It is not hard 
to imagine that all these peculiarities of the Hebrew verb make 
the translators’ work difficult, though they can at the same 
time be an abundant source of nuances that enrich the exegesis 
of the sacred texts. 
Furthermore, the Hebrew verb has an imperative equivalent to that of 
our Spanish language; two infinitives (absolute and construct), the 
first of which is simply a verbal noun used 
very frequently with a conjugated verb to reinforce the 
meaning of the action (cf. in Genesis 2:17 God’s warning to 
the newly created man regarding the tree of the knowledge of good and 
evil, «you shall surely die», lit. «dying you shall die», moth tamuth), 
while the second corresponds exactly to our 
infinitive; and a participle that indicates the agent, the one who performs the 
action (the one who calls, the one who speaks, the one who listens), as in the well-known 
words that introduce Psalm 23, literally «Yahweh is the one who 
shepherds me», roí. That is why many participles are understood 
simply as nouns.   
2. Noun. As in many other languages of the world, the 
noun in Hebrew designates real or imaginary beings, as well as 
abstract qualities, anthroponyms, and toponyms. From the 
point of view of gender it can only be masculine or feminine, 
according to the usual grammars; in reality, one should rather say 
“marked” and “unmarked”, since the feminine also encompasses 
what in other languages is considered the neuter gender. And it admits 
three numbers: singular, plural, and dual, the last of restricted use 
and reserved for entities that come in pairs in the natural world 
(hands, eyes, feet, etc.). The masculine singular noun is very 
variable, while the feminine singular is usually characterized 
(though not always) by the ending –ah. The masculine plural has 
as its proper ending the form –im and the feminine plural the form –
12

oth, though there may be exceptions. Duals, which designate two 
things, two persons, two related concepts, are distinguished by their 
ending in –áyim or –tháyim, depending on whether they are masculine 
or feminine duals. Determination of the noun is effected by means of the 
article ha- or also written, always prefixed as a constitutive morpheme 
(it is not a separate word as in Spanish) and 
invariable for all genders and numbers, e.g. berith “covenant”, 
habberith “the covenant”. As for case, the Hebrew noun does not present 
a declension similar to that of Latin, Greek, or other languages; 
it simply preserves remnants of the ancient Semitic declension in 
some particular morphemes. The only outstanding case is what 
grammarians call the construct relationship, equivalent to the genitive or 
determinative complement of other languages; the only difference 
lies in that the possessor remains in the general form (or absolute 
state), while what is possessed takes a different form (or construct 
state). Let us see an example: «Law» is said in Hebrew torah (absolute 
state). If we want to say «the Law of Moses», the word «Law», which 
is what is possessed, takes a different form torath, in the construct state, 
while the name of Moses remains unaltered, in the absolute 
state, that is, torath Mosheh, the opposite of what happens in our languages: in 
Spanish the name of the possessor appears determined by the 
preposition of and in languages with declension in the genitive case. Hebrew 
construct states are very variable in their morphology; one cannot 
offer a fixed ending that covers them as a whole. In 
most cases they are indicated simply by vocalic alterations and are evident by their position in the whole of the nominal 
phrase (always in first place). 
3. Adjectives. Surprisingly, the Hebrew language is very poor 
in adjectives. This is because in the verbal conjugation there exist roots that 
by themselves express the idea of “to be great”, “to be small”, “to be 
strong”, “to be weak”, “to be tall”, “to be short”, etc. They are not, therefore, 
as necessary as in other languages. 
4. Pronouns. Hebrew presents a highly developed series of personal pronouns, 
in which only those of the first person 
serve for both genders (aní or anokhí, I; najnú or anajnú, 
we, interchangeably), while those of the second and third 
distinguish a masculine and a feminine form (atah, you, man; at, 
you, woman; atem, you [masc. pl.]; atenah, you [fem. pl.]; hú, he; hí, she; hem or 
13

hemmah, they [masc.]; hen or hennah, they [fem.]). It also offers an invariable relative pronoun 
for all genders and numbers (asher, that, which), 
a series of demonstratives or deictics that distinguish masculine and feminine gender, 
singular and plural (zeh, this [masc.]; zoth, this [fem.]; el·leh, 
these [masc. or fem.], interchangeably; on the other hand, the third-person personal pronouns 
also function as remote deictics, with the meanings 
of “that”, “those”, “yon”, etc.), and a wide range of interrogatives and indefinites, among 
which stand out common nouns used with indefinite 
value, such as, e.g., ish or nephesh, “man” and “soul”, 
respectively, with the meaning of “someone”, “anyone”, “whoever”, 
or similar. Furthermore, the Hebrew language possesses a whole system of pronominal suffixes 
of the second and third grammatical persons in their different genders and numbers 
(those of the first are invariable) that serve to indicate 
possession and function both with the noun and with the verb.  
5. Relating particles. The Hebrew prepositional system is 
very poor, with three multipurpose prefixes of use similar to the 
article, be- (locative and instrumental), k- (comparative, associative), and l- 
(destinative), and very few prepositions understood as such, which 
as often happens in other languages are simply ancient 
fossilized nouns with a specialized use: el, toward; ben, in the midst 
of; al, above, upon; etc. As for nexuses or conjunctions, there are 
also very few, the most important of which is the prefix we- 
or simply u-, with polyvalent meaning: it can be 
copulative, adversative, disjunctive, final, consecutive, etc. Hence 
the difficulty of its translation and the variety of interpretations 
that can thereby be given to certain clauses.  
6. Syntax. The syntax of Hebrew is very simple because of the great 
freedom with which the different elements appear in the sentence. The 
main one is always placed at the beginning and is usually the verb, followed 
by the subject and the direct object. All the same, if the author wishes 
to highlight a concept in a special way, he may very well place it in 
first position, or in vedette, as one says, whatever it may be; this 
alteration of habitual syntax is usually more frequent in poetry, 
such as the Psalms or the book of Job. Particular characteristics of 
Hebrew syntax are the construct relationship we saw in the section 
on the noun, the characteristic particle for distinguishing determined 
14

direct objects eth (only in good prose, never in poetry), the 
absolute infinitive to reinforce verbal action, and the so-called consecutive 
waw, of which we have already spoken above.

lessons.title: The Aramaic Language
lessons.subtitle: Use in Daniel, Ezra, and the NT

content:
In some older manuals it is still called the Chaldean language 
or simply Chaldee, which is in reality the designation of one 
of its historical dialects, that of Babylon or Chaldea. 
Aramaic is a Northwestern Semitic language related to 
Hebrew and Phoenician. In its origin it was the dialect of the tribes that around 
the year 1300 B.C. entered the Syro-Palestinian region, founding 
several cities there. The Aramaic language is thus documented from 
the second millennium before Christ. In the Bible there remains a trace of the 
Aramaic of those remote times in the notice that Laban, uncle 
of Jacob, designated by the name Yegar Sahadutha the monument 
erected to commemorate the covenant with Jacob, a cairn which the latter called 
in Hebrew Gilead (cf. Gen. 31:47).  
The importance of Aramaic as a language lies in that it came to 
be the commercial language of the Fertile Crescent, its use spreading 
further into Egypt, the Arabian peninsula, Iran, Central Asia, and 
India from the 6th century B.C. owing to the influence of the Persian 
Empire, which adopted it as an administrative language. Written documents and monumental 
inscriptions bear witness to this. But already two centuries earlier it had attained the rank of 
diplomatic language of the Near East, knowledge of which was 
indispensable for the upper classes, as 2 Kgs. 18:26 shows us.  
Aramaic evolved and diversified into various dialects. It is 
usually classified for study into three phases: Old Aramaic, Middle 
(or Classical, within which Biblical Aramaic is found), and Modern. 
Like the other Semitic languages it is characterized by the 
triliteralism of verbal roots and by the preponderance of 
consonants over vowels. The Aramaic alephbet in no way differs from the 
Hebrew; in fact, what we call the “Hebrew alephbet” is in reality the 
Aramaic alephbet, adopted by the Jews from the Babylonian captivity 
onward, as they gradually abandoned their ancestral language to 
replace it with Aramaic. The Aramaic language was much more flexible 
than Hebrew, better suited to expressing the nuances and circumstances 
of a narrative or the developments of thought. Toward the end of 
Persian rule coins were minted in Palestine on which appears 
E 
16

only the word Yehud, Judea, in Aramaic script. In the Hellenistic period 
the majority of Jews already spoke Aramaic as their own language and 
intensified its use in daily life in order to resist the pressure 
of Hellenic culture and customs, Hebrew remaining as 
lingua sacra, that is, reserved for the reading of the Scriptures, the 
commentaries and discussions of the synagogue schools (though highly 
Aramaized in this last case) and, perhaps, as the language of the home 
among aristocratic and priestly families. From this period date 
several commentaries on the Jewish Scriptures written in the Aramaic 
language, the Targums.  
The parts of the Old Testament that were composed 
directly in Aramaic are: Ezra 4:8–6:18; 7:12–26; Daniel 2:4b–
7:28; Jeremiah 10:11 and two words of Genesis 31:47. The truth is that 
in the time of Jesus the Aramaic language was the habitual vehicle of 
familial and commercial expression among the Jews.  
With regard to the New Testament, while the debate remains open 
among scholars concerning a supposed (and traditional) 
first Aramaic composition of the Gospel according to Saint Matthew—or 
Hebrew, according to M. Grintz, C. Tresmontant, and others—the truth is that 
we find several purely Aramaic expressions on the lips of Jesus 
recorded in the Gospels: Talitha qumi, Abba, Ephphata, and Eloí, Eloí, 
lama sabactani. This would mean that Christ’s mother tongue would be, 
without any doubt, the Galilean variant of Palestinian Aramaic. All this, 
together with the fact that in some Pauline epistles evident 
Aramaisms are preserved, such as Abba or maranatha, has led some 
researchers to uphold the theory of a first Aramaic drafting 
of the four Gospels and of the Pauline corpus. What these 
Aramaisms in reality show is the evidence of a clear 
Palestinian origin of Christianity and of an oral tradition which, though 
expressed in the Greek language in communities of pagan origin, 
faithfully preserved sayings of the Lord or of the first Jewish disciples 
in their original Aramaic language.  
In the Jewish religious sphere, as we have noted, Hebrew continued to 
be preserved in the learned discussions of Scripture, 
though highly Aramaized. Nevertheless, the commentary on the Mishnah, 
«repetition», a body of laws emanating from Jewish teaching or «oral 
law», which sought to respond to the changing needs of the 
life of faithful Israelites, was already written in Aramaic and received the 
17

name of Gemara. The Mishnah, plus its commentary or Gemara, 
received the name of Talmud, «teaching», a collective work of which 
there are two versions, that of Jerusalem and that of Babylon.  
Aramaic, especially in its variant called Syriac, managed to 
maintain itself as the language of the Eastern peoples against the cultural 
pressure of Greek in antiquity, so that those 
societies were practically bilingual. But it could not withstand the Arabic 
wave that spread through the Near East from the 7th century of 
our era. The Jewish inhabitants of Palestine, who nevertheless preserved 
their Aramaic language as a distinctive mark amid medieval Arab and then Turkish 
domination until 1918, and who lent themselves to interesting studies carried out by European scholars, 
since the founding of the present state of Israel have been diluting their 
ancestral language into the present Neo-Hebrew or ibrit, so that today 
that rich Jewish Aramaic variant practically no longer exists.     
In the Eastern Christian sphere Aramaic was preserved during 
the first centuries of our era under the name of Syriac, 
the designation of one of its dialects, specifically that spoken in 
Syria, and despite competition from Greek it produced within itself an 
excellent biblical version, the Peshitta, as well as a whole patristic 
literature, whose most conspicuous representative was Ephrem the Syrian. 
Considered moreover as the official language of some churches of Eastern 
rite, it has remained alive to our day in the 
Maronite Christian communities of Syria and Lebanon, among the 
Mandaeans of Iraq and Iran, and the so-called “Malabar Christians” or 
“Christians of Saint Thomas” of India. Nevertheless, the largest 
Aramaic-speaking community is found among Christians of 
Syrian origin residing in the United States, to whom Mel 
Gibson turned when drafting the screenplay of his controversial film The 
Passion of the Christ, shot basically in Aramaic. The determination with which 
speakers of this language continue to maintain it in their families and in 
their churches as their own distinctive mark, together with the access they have given it 
to new technologies (the Internet), augurs its preservation for 
several centuries more, even though today it has no 
recognition as an official language in any modern state.  
With regard to its grammar, Biblical Aramaic presents a 
system similar to that of Hebrew grammar. The variants that exist 
in verbal conjugation or the inflection of nouns are of the same 
18

type as may exist between related languages of our great 
Romance family, as, for example, between Spanish and Italian, 
or Spanish and Catalan, or Spanish and Galician or Portuguese.

What concept or passage from this lesson was most significant to you? Explain why.
How can you apply what you have learned in your personal life or in your service in the church?
What questions remain after this reading? What would you like to explore further?
Prepare to share with your group: a key takeaway from «Biblical texts in Aramaic».

lessons.title: The Greek Language
lessons.subtitle: Koine and the translation of the Scriptures

content:
Greek, called by its speakers in antiquity the «Hellenic 
language» or helleniké glossa (eliniká in modern Greek), is today 
one of the best-documented languages in the 
world: its evolution can be followed for more than three thousand years, 
from the Mycenaean tablets of the 2nd millennium B.C. to the latest edition 
of any newspaper, television or radio program, or to the latest 
contribution made by the Internet in present-day Greece, where it remains 
a living language, its official language, as well as in part of the island of 
Cyprus and southern Italy.

Greek forms part of the Indo-European linguistic family (which 
some German authors still prefer to designate today as 
Indo-Germanic), originating from the steppes of Central Asia, and which in the 
5th millennium B.C. begins to penetrate Europe, reaching the 
Balkan peninsula and the Aegean Sea around the middle of the 4th millennium. The 
range of branches of this family is enormous, distributed in two 
groups:

1. Balto-Slavic, from which derive the Baltic languages, the most 
important of which is Lithuanian or Žemaitian, followed by Latvian and 
Old Prussian, extinct since the 18th century, as well as the great Slavic family, 
within which we highlight liturgical Slavic, Russian, which is 
the most important in extent, Ukrainian, Polish, Belarusian, 
Czech, Slovak, Bulgarian, and Serbo-Croatian.  
2. Illyrian, from which present-day Albanian derives. 
3. Anatolian, whose most outstanding representatives are Thracian and 
Phrygian, both languages dead since antiquity. 
4. Armenian, from which present-day Armenian derives, closely related 
to Greek.  
E 
20

5. Indo-Iranian, a fruitful branch that gave rise to Persian or Iranian with 
its dialects, to Sanskrit, the sacred language of the Hindus, to Vedic and 
all the Indo-European languages spoken today in India, the most 
important of which is Hindi, which has the rank of official language 
in that immense country.  
6. Hittite-Luwian, a linguistic group that has left no 
survivors at present, but that knew a certain importance 
in antiquity. Hittite is its most conspicuous representative. 
7. Greek. Although there are authors who tend to see in it a 
language of Western type, many place it in the Eastern 
group and note its great similarities with Armenian, 
Indo-Iranian, or Balto-Slavic. 
Second, the Western group, also called centum:

1. Germanic, from which derive Old Gothic with its 
dialects and the present Scandinavian languages (Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, 
Faroese, Icelandic), English, German with its dialects, Saxon, Frisian, and 
Dutch with its Dutch and Flemish (or Belgian) variants. 
2. Venetic, extinguished around the 1st century of our era. 
3. Celtic, a fruitful branch that has given a good linguistic offspring: 
ancient Gaulish and ancient Celtiberian of the Iberian peninsula, both 
extinct; Cornish of the British southwest (Cornwall peninsula) which has dragged on 
on the brink of extinction since the 18th century, 
and present-day Gaelic with its variants of Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, as well 
as Breton of northwestern France.  
4. Italic, from which proceed the ancient Oscan, Umbrian, Sabine, 
Faliscan, and the most important of all, Latin, mother of the present 
Romance languages: Spanish, Portuguese, Galician, French, Catalan, Occitan, 
Italian, Sardinian, Rhaeto-Romance, and Romanian, each with its own variants and 
dialects. Dalmatian, a Balkan Romance language, became extinct 
at the end of the 19th century. 
5. Tocharian. This name designates a set of languages and 
dialects spoken in Chinese Turkestan (Xinjiang) until the 8th century 
A.D., the most important of which are Tocharian proper 
and Kuchean, which became extinct when their speakers were assimilated 
21

by other tribes and other cultures. Although these are languages spoken 
in the East, they are included with regard to linguistics in the Western 
group because they share their features with the Western languages.  
 History of the Greek language

1. Mycenaean period. Located toward the second half of the 2nd 
millennium B.C., the only documents preserved are clay tablets that have 
come down to us thanks to the fires that 
destroyed the Mycenaean palaces (Mycenae, Pylos, Tiryns, Crete), 
which fixed them forever by baking them. The language that appears in 
them, catalogued as Linear B and deciphered by Michael Ventris in 
1952, is an ancient variant of Greek written by means of a 
syllabary adapted from other languages unknown to us, and 
which informs us of the entries and exits of the palaces and temples 
of that remote Hellenic world. Most of the terms 
used in those tablets will later be found in Homer and in the 
classical language, many of them even reaching modern Greek. 
2. Dark Age. The destruction of Mycenaean civilization by 
the Dorians and the so-called Sea Peoples in the 12th century B.C. plunges 
Greece into a supposed period of illiteracy lasting more or 
less until the 8th or 7th centuries B.C. Since we possess today 
no written documentation whatever from this period, the most 
accepted hypothesis is that culture must have been transmitted orally, of which 
we find evidence in the fact that ancient traditions 
concerning the Mycenaean world (the Trojan War, the voyage of the 
Argonauts, the expedition of the Seven against Thebes, the cycle of 
Heracles, the legends about Theseus, etc.) survived until they were 
put into writing in subsequent periods.   
3. Earliest poets. Homer, traditional composer of the Iliad and 
the Odyssey, and Hesiod, author of the Theogony and Works and Days, are 
the first bards who produce their work in the Greek language in an 
undetermined epoch, but which tradition places between the 8th and 7th centuries 
B.C. Homer’s dialect is an artificial mixture for poetic use 
22

of the Ionic and Aeolic dialects. Hesiod composes rather in Old Ionic. 
4. Classical period. It extends from the 6th to the 4th century B.C. and is the 
moment when the Greek language reaches its greatest splendor. 
Fragmented into five dialectal groups (Aeolic, Doric, Ionic-Attic, 
Arcado-Cypriot, and Northwestern dialects), it knows a great 
literary production that lays the foundations of the culture and 
thought of the West: on the island Aeolic Alcaeus and Sappho compose their poems; 
the Doric dialect is ennobled by the poetic work of 
Alcman; Ionic sees in the statesman Solon and the historian Herodotus its 
principal representatives; and Attic, transformed by the political 
influence of Athens into classical Greek par excellence, leaps onto the 
stage of art with the three great tragedians Aeschylus, Sophocles, 
and Euripides, and the comic Aristophanes; it dominates the field of history 
with Thucydides, and in Plato it is consecrated as the language of philosophy 
and thought. 
5. Koine Greek. The pan-Hellenic policy of Philip of Macedon 
and the conquests of his son Alexander the Great in the East open to 
the Attic dialect from the end of the 4th century B.C. a horizon far more 
vast than Athens could ever have dreamed. The dialect of 
Athens, thus placed in permanent contact with the other Greek dialects 
and also with other peoples and other very different languages, 
adapts to the new situation and is slowly transformed, losing 
in purity and classical correctness, but gaining in vocabulary and conceptual 
richness. The name Koine Greek or “common” Greek is given to this new 
language that little by little eliminates the ancient historical dialectal speech 
of Hellas and becomes the cultural and 
economic vehicle of the ancient world, from India to Rome and the 
West, on the one hand, and from the steppes of Central Asia to 
Egypt and Nubia, on the other, and that remains as such at least 
until the 6th century of our era. In it historians such as 
Xenophon and Polybius express themselves, philosophers such as Aristotle and Plotinus, scientists 
such as Theophrastus of Alexandria, poets such as Menander and Apollonius of 
Rhodes, biographers such as Plutarch, and the whole host of literati, sages, 
and technicians of the later Hellenistic world. Even an emperor so 
Roman as Hadrian prefers the Koine Greek language for writing his 
most intimate thoughts. In the first centuries of the Christian era 
the Atticist movement, advocated by authors such as Dionysius of 
23

Halicarnassus or Lucian, among others, seeks to make Greek 
return to its original Attic purity, but it remains no more than an attempt 
limited to literary circles. Within Koine Greek special attention is due to 
what we call Biblical Greek, which we reserve because of its 
importance for a later section.  
6. Byzantine Greek. It extends from the 6th century to the 15th century A.D. 
and is also known as Medieval Greek. It is in substance Koine Greek 
limited to the increasingly restricted frontiers of the Eastern 
Roman Empire, later known as the Byzantine Empire, and 
subjected to new influences, especially Slavic. Its greatest 
literary production, which represents a great regression in relation to the 
previous stage, is erudite and theological: in it the fathers and 
thinking heads of the Greek Orthodox Church of the Middle Ages express themselves, 
such as Saint John of Damascus. Its derivation is 
7. Modern Greek, which extends from the fall of 
Constantinople into Turkish hands in 1453 to our day. The 
present language, formed through the long period in which Greece 
was subject to Ottoman power (1453–1829; some Greek territories 
remained in Turkish hands practically until 1918), 
shows great foreign influences, basically Turkish and Slavic, 
but also Italian and French, Venice being the great commercial 
power in the medieval and modern Eastern Mediterranean, and 
France throughout the 19th century and early 20th setting the pattern of 
European culture. The modern Greek language oscillates between two 
antagonistic tendencies: the purist, which advocates a type of language 
that imitates as far as possible the ancient language, called for that reason katharévousa, 
that is, pure, and the popular movement, which defends the normal 
evolution of the language, that is, dimotikí or the language of the people. Although 
the latter has the rank of official language in Greece and Cyprus since 
1974, the Orthodox Church, the most cultivated writers, and scientists 
still tend to prefer katharévousa for their 
publications to this day, as do political leaders of more 
conservative ideas. All the same, dimotikí gains ground even in 
these areas; by way of example we may say that the Bible published 
in Greek in 1997 by the Hellenic Bible Societies, although 
it shows letters of ecclesiastical recommendation in katharévousa, contains 
the sacred text already in dimotikí. Modern Greek has at 
present some twenty-five million speakers distributed 
24

among Greece, Cyprus, southern Italy (the Taranto area), and the colonies 
of Hellenic immigrants scattered through Western Europe and the 
American hemisphere, basically, and it also has its dialects: 
Tsakonian, a remnant of ancient Doric spoken in the territory of 
ancient Sparta or Laconia (now Tsakonia); Pontic, a modality 
proper to the Greeks of the Anatolian Black Sea coast, most 
of whom now reside in northern present-day Greece, owing to the 
deportations and population transfers that took place between 
Hellenes and Turks after the First World War; and the dialects 
of southern Italy, which are written not with the Greek alphabet but with the 
Latin one. 
 The Greek alphabet

It is of Phoenician origin, Semitic therefore, and was introduced into 
Greece around the 8th or 7th centuries B.C. It consists of 24 letters, vowels and 
consonants, with distinction of uppercase and lowercase:

alpha (a) 
 beta (b). In modern Greek vita (fricative v, as in French or in 
literary Catalan) 
 gamma (voiced g) 
 delta (d, in modern Greek always fricative d)  
 epsilon (e) 
 zeta (ds). In modern Greek zita (voiced s) 
 eta (long e). In modern Greek ita (i) 
 theta (th). In modern Greek thita 
 iota (i) 
 kappa (k) 
 lambda (l) 
 mu (m) 
 nu (n) 
25

xi (x) 
 omicron (o) 
 pi (p) 
 rho (r, in modern Greek always a single tap)  
 sigma (voiceless s), with a final form 
 tau (t). In modern Greek tav 
 upsilon (ü, in modern Greek i) 
 phi (ph) 
 chi (kh) 
 psi (ps) 
 omega (long o, in modern Greek normal o) 
In antiquity only capital or 
uppercase letters were used, later called uncials. The lowercase is of 
medieval origin.  
In the beginning the Greek alphabet had other letters that were not 
always used by all Hellenes, of dialectal use until the 
7th and 6th centuries B.C., such as sampi, digamma, stigma, qoppa, or san. Of all 
of them digamma (
 ) is of the greatest phonological value, equivalent to the 
phoneme /w/, of great extent in certain dialects such as Doric and 
Aeolic; qoppa represented the phoneme /q/ of the Semitic languages, 
sampi or disigma a phoneme /hs/, stigma the /ts/ that we find, for 
example, in Biblical Hebrew, and san was a graphic variant of the 
phoneme /s/. Also falling into disuse was a way of writing the letter 
sigma used in Alexandrian Koine and in Byzantine Greek whose 
grapheme was identical to our letter c, and which has remained as a legacy 
in the Slavic Cyrillic alphabet with the phonetic value of [s].  
The ancient Greeks, like most peoples, 
also used their alphabet as numerical signs. The Greeks 
of today, on the other hand, have adopted Arabic numerals.  
26

The signs that usually accompany our printed texts of 
today (acute, grave, and circumflex accents, as well as the spirits, rough 
and smooth) to indicate elevation of tone or aspirations, saw the light 
in Alexandria, during the Hellenistic period. Modern Greek, in 
its dimotikí variant, has eliminated them entirely, leaving 
only the acute accent; katharévousa, however, maintains 
them all, though in pronunciation it does not distinguish them.

As we have indicated above, Biblical Greek is to be located 
in time within the Koine period. By it we understand the 
level of the Greek language employed for the drafting or translation of 
the Sacred Texts. In this sense, we must make a distinction 
between the Greek of the Septuagint and the Greek of the New Testament:

1. The Greek of the Septuagint is clearly a translation Greek for the exclusive use of Jews and proselytes of Judaism, in 
which the effort to maintain the original expression of the Hebrew 
texts of the Old Testament generates a type of syntax very alien 
to classical prose; by way of example, literal calques of Hebrew sentences are frequent, 
with the verb in first position (in 
vedette), followed by the subject: en arkhê epoíesen ho theós ton uranón 
kai ten gen (Gen 1:1); kai ekáthissen Abessalom (2 Sam 14:28), etc. (the 
boldface is ours); likewise, Semitic words abound that are not 
translated but simply adapted phonetically to the Greek alphabet, and that must have been decidedly incomprehensible to 
those not in contact with Jewish culture and religion: 
gabin (2 Kgs 25:12), kinyra (1 Sam 10:5), paskha (Ex. 12:11), etc. 
2. The Greek of the New Testament is, on the contrary, an 
original production at very different levels in which, alongside the 
higher and more cultivated Koine language (Epistle to the Hebrews, 
Pauline correspondence, Lucan work), we find another very similar to that of 
the contemporary Egyptian papyri, such as those discovered at 
Oxyrhynchus at the end of the 19th century (Gospel of Mark); alongside a 
genuinely classical syntax (genitives absolute, eti autû laluntos, 
Luke 8:49; appositive participles, aphorismenos eis euangelion theû, Rom 
1:1) we find deliberate calques of the Semitic constructions 
proper to the Hebrew Masoretic Text or to the Septuagint (verb in 
27

vedette followed by the subject, kaí érkhetai he méter autû, Mark 3:31); alongside 
clearly Greek terms (the overwhelming majority) appear others 
that are Latin (kustodía, spekulátor, sudarion) and an important number 
of Semitisms, combined according to each author’s personal style 
(sábbaton, Satanâs, talitha). The idea maintained by some philologists 
of the past, according to which New Testament Greek is of inferior 
quality or even decadent in comparison with the great authors 
of the classical period, lacks weight today when one sees how the 
sacred authors wrote not only according to their personal linguistic capacities, 
but also following a preconceived plan to which they 
adhered strictly. Thus, e.g., the Gospel according to Saint Luke, 
reputed as one of the works of the best linguistic level in the New 
Testament, offers throughout its detailed narrative of Jesus’ ministry 
constructions similar to those of the Athenian historian 
Thucydides, together with a deliberate imitation of the 
Semitizing style of the LXX, the Bible of all Greek-speaking believers, 
in the first two chapters, in which it narrates the birth 
and childhood of the Lord; it is evident that the evangelist understands this 
birth as rooted in the sacred traditions of Israel, 
and therefore relates it in a Semitizing style, while he conceives the 
teaching ministry of Christ as a projection of Divine Wisdom 
to the Hellenic-speaking world, the Gentiles, whence his more 
classical style. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, who does not hesitate to cite 
literally or paraphrase the Septuagint when it suits the 
development of his discourse, does not hide his diction and his purely Alexandrian 
syntax, with a style that we find in Philo and other 
authors from Hellenistic Egypt. The Gospel according to Saint 
Mark, considered today as one of the best exponents of what 
spoken Koine must have been, plays masterfully with Semitic 
diction, so that he knows how to transmit to an audience of Hellenic language 
and culture a highly colorful picture of what Jesus’ ministry in Palestine was, 
even transcribing the ipsissima verba Domini («the original word of the Lord») in Aramaic. And the 
Apocalypse of Saint John, to cite but one last example, 
traditionally stigmatized as a poorly written work by someone 
who did not express himself well in Greek, evidences such a mastery of 
Hellenic syntax that it has nothing to envy of any classical author; 
moreover, its supposed «incorrectnesses» are seen today as a 
deliberate effort to call attention to certain sacred names and 
denominations that the author wishes to highlight, very much in 
28

keeping with his Jewish origins. We cannot doubt that 
both Jesus and the apostles, Israelites originally from Galilee, a bilingual 
region, must have been perfectly competent in both Aramaic 
and Greek, with a passive knowledge, no doubt, of the Hebrew language, 
considered as lingua sacra. The New Testament reflects 
this particularity by transmitting the Good News in a perfect 
Koine Greek with an indelible Jewish imprint.

We highlight below the proper features of the Greek language 
in general lines, emphasizing, however, the 
most outstanding characteristics of Biblical Greek. 
1. Verb. The verb is the most important part of Greek grammar 
because of its intrinsic richness. It offers two systems of 
conjugation, in –mi, 
 , and in –o, 
 , the first more ancient and 
almost totally displaced in the Koine by the second; in fact, the 
New Testament scarcely presents examples of the first type, except 
the verb eimí, 
 , the copulative verb (to be), the only one of this 
group that has reached modern Greek. We find in the 
Greek verb three voices, active, middle, and passive, the last two of which 
merge into one in the Koine, and four fundamental themes 
in which one tense and three kinds of action are reflected: 
present theme (durative action), aorist theme (punctual action), perfect theme 
(present result of a past action), and future theme 
(future time); the basic opposition is made by the present and 
aorist themes; the perfect theme already shows signs of weakness in the Koine and the 
future theme did not prosper in the course of the language. For example, of the 
regular verb lýo, 
 , “to untie, ransom, liberate”, the themes are the 
following:  
Present theme lýo, 
 , “to be untying”  
Aorist theme élysa, 
 , “to untie” 
Perfect theme lélyka, 
 , “to have untied” 
Future theme lyso, 
 , “to be going to untie”.  
In modern Greek only the basic opposition functions, present and 
aorist; the future tense is periphrastic, as is the perfect, that is, 
29

it is formed by means of auxiliaries. As for verbal tenses, 
the Greek verb has: present, imperfect, aorist (equivalent to our 
preterite indefinite or simple past perfect), future, perfect, 
pluperfect, and future perfect, distributed among the moods 
indicative, subjunctive, imperative, and optative, the last a special mood 
to indicate wish. As nominal forms it presents 
infinitives and an abundant quantity of participles. In the Koine the optative mood 
falls into disuse and only achieves an artificial resurgence with 
the Atticists, and the future perfect tense is almost never used. In fact, the 
New Testament offers us very few examples of either.  
2. Noun. We include in this category those traditionally designated 
as substantive noun and adjective noun. The noun 
in Greek designates real or fictitious entities and bears the three classical genders: 
masculine, feminine, and neuter, and three numbers: singular, plural, and 
dual, the last for beings that in reality present themselves in pairs 
(hands, feet, eyes, horses of a team), though from the classical period 
it tends to be replaced by the plural; in fact, it is not found in the 
Koine. As for its morphology, the Greek noun fits into three 
models of declension: thematic, athematic, and a-stem, of which 
the first is the most productive and the second the most 
complicated, so that it will disappear as the language 
evolves. In fact, modern Greek maintains the thematic declension and the 
a-stem; of the athematic declension there remain 
only scarce residues. The tendency toward regularization of 
nominal paradigms is a patent reality in the Koine, as 
the New Testament evidences. There are five cases of the declension:

Nominative (case of the subject and nominal predicate)  
Vocative (case of exclamation or apostrophe) 
Accusative (case of the direct object and of direction)  
Genitive (case of the determinative complement and of origin)  
Dative (case of the indirect object and of the instrumental)  
In the New Testament, as in the Koine in general, the case 
system maintains the classical forms, though subtle changes are evident that will lead to the case opposition of modern Greek: 
subject case (nominative) versus regimen case (accusative); in modern Greek 
30

the genitive has a very restricted use and the dative has 
disappeared completely, except in katharévousa. On the contrary, 
the present language has developed in a completely 
extraordinary way the use of the vocative, which both in the Koine and in the 
classical language had a rather mediocre existence. 
3. Pronoun. The Greek language enormously developed the 
pronominal system, both with regard to personal pronouns, and with regard to demonstratives, relatives, or 
indefinites, which present the same system of declension as the 
noun, with the same genders, numbers, and cases. An important appendix 
is that of the ancient deictic ho, he, to 
 , which in classical Attic 
is transformed into the article and direct determiner of the noun, 
a function with which it passes into the Koine and is maintained in present-day Greek. 
4. Relators. The system of prepositions and conjunctions is 
highly developed in the Greek language from Homeric poems. The classical language offers a perfect systematization of 
prepositions, distributing them among three cases: accusative, 
genitive, and dative. In the Koine the process of reinforcing 
the classical prepositions begins, and a certain instability as to the 
cases they govern, as the New Testament well evidences. Modern Greek 
has reduced the prepositions to the accusative case. The 
conjunctions or nexuses of the classical language function with a great 
precision that begins to blur in the Koine. In the present language 
they are much reduced. 
5. Syntax. The Greek language presents great flexibility in 
its constructions, as its whole history evidences, always giving 
priority in the sentence to the word or words one wishes to 
highlight; the more or less habitual order has usually been from the most ancient 
times to its present-day employment

Proper features of classical Greek syntax are the use of sentences 
with the verb in the optative dependent on past tenses, what is 
known by the name of oblique optative or oblique subordination; the 
constructions of infinitive with subject in the accusative and, above all, the 
varied participle constructions (attributive, appositive, and 
predicative), among which the so-called genitive absolute stands out, that is, 
31

a participle and a noun, both in the genitive, with a certain 
independence within the whole of the grammatical sentence, the closest thing to our absolute constructions in literary Spanish 
(once the lecture concluded, the session was adjourned), all forms 
that allow great flexibility of expression. Although the first 
two become very restricted in the Koine, especially 
oblique subordination, which is almost nonexistent, participial constructions 
survive even in the New Testament, though somewhat 
nuanced. None of all this remains in modern Greek. The 
New Testament texts offer us examples of simple syntax, 
proper to the spoken language (Gospel of Saint Mark), as well as of 
the most elaborate, of the school, with literary figures of the highest level 
(Saint Paul, Saint Luke, Epistle to the Hebrews). And as we have already 
noted in its time, it presents in some books, such as the 
Gospels, a deliberate Semitizing style that becomes very patent 
in a peculiar syntax, a calque of the Septuagint and of the Hebrew 
texts of the Old Testament, with the verb in first position 
followed by the subject, the so-called graphic participles (in which the 
participle accompanies the main verb, not to express a concrete nuance 
referring to the subject or the object, but as if of two concomitant actions 
it were a matter. Cf. the construction going out they went, of 
Mark 1:29), a special syndetic concatenation of sentences by 
means of the copulative conjunction kai 
 , the use of the word son 
plus qualitative genitive to express traits proper to a person 
(sons of iniquity for iniquitous, sons of light for faithful, etc.), the superfluous 
use of personal pronouns in the genitive or dative where 
Hebrew verbs employ suffixes, etc., features that are also 
proper to the more popular Koine diction and that survive in many 
cases in the present language.  
All this contributes to making the Greek language of the New 
Testament a language especially suited to transmit the conceptual 
richness of the Gospel, with a literary dress that makes it 
one of the masterpieces of human literature of all 
times.
